COMPLIANCE GAP ANALYSIS MEMORANDUM

To:      Engagement File — Healthcare Life Sciences
From:    Healthcare Regulatory / Data Privacy Counsel
Re:      HIPAA Compliance Program Gap Analysis; Reconciliation of Counterparty Markup Deviations
Date:    [Engagement Date]
Output:  compliance-gap-memorandum.docx

================================================================================
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
================================================================================

This memorandum reviews the client's Healthcare Data Privacy Compliance Program materials in the healthcare life sciences matter and identifies program deficiencies, residual risks, and recommended remediation under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended, and its implementing regulations (collectively, "HIPAA"), including the Privacy Rule, Security Rule, and Breach Notification Rule (45 C.F.R. Parts 160 and 164), as well as applicable state consumer health-data and breach-notification requirements that operate alongside HIPAA.

Separately, this memorandum reconciles the counterparty's latest markup against the base deal materials and the controlling disclosure schedules and exhibits. Every identified deviation is addressed below. Scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials.

Principal findings:

1. Program gaps exist across governance, workforce training, business associate management, risk analysis / risk management, access controls and audit logging, breach incident response, and right-of-access / individual-rights workflows. Several gaps create elevated OCR enforcement and contractual indemnification exposure.

2. The counterparty markup introduces three material deviations from firm-standard / base materials: (a) a silent reduction of the indemnification cap coupled with conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket; (b) Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") carve-outs for regulatory action of the type implicated by this matter; and (c) a shortened survival / limitation period for core representations. Each deviation intersects scheduled disclosures and must be treated as open risk unless expressly accepted.

3. Recommended path: close HIPAA program gaps on a time-bound remediation plan; reject or heavily condition the survival-period reduction and the MAE regulatory carve-outs as drafted; quantify and re-paper the indemnification economics so that Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities are not silently shifted; and preserve Exhibit B survival matrix alignment for privacy, security, and compliance representations.

================================================================================
II. SCOPE, SOURCES, AND METHODOLOGY
================================================================================

A. In-Scope Materials (Operative)

- Deal materials — healthcare-life-sciences analyze: Healthcare Data Privacy Compliance Program Gap (base / operative record).
- Counterparty markup — healthcare-life-sciences analyze: Healthcare Data Privacy Compliance P (deviations to reconcile against base).
- Schedules and exhibits — healthcare-life-sciences (qualifying the base; scheduled exceptions control): Schedule 3.7 (pending regulatory inquiries); Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities); Exhibit B (survival matrix).

B. Out-of-Scope / Do Not Rely

- Misfiled correspondence and materials from unrelated engagements (including corporate-governance matter files sharing similar titles). Those records are not operative for this analysis and have not been relied upon.
- Superseded internal priority statements, if any, that conflict with the operative base materials, markup, and schedules.

C. Analytical Framework

Gap analysis maps program elements to HIPAA regulatory requirements and common OCR resolution-agreement expectations, then rates each gap by:

- Deficiency (what is missing or non-conforming);
- Risk (enforcement, contractual, operational, and deal-economics exposure);
- Remediation (concrete corrective action, owner-role expectation, and sequencing).

Markup reconciliation maps each counterparty deviation to the affected base provision, the intersecting schedule/exhibit, residual risk if accepted as drafted, and a recommended negotiating position.

================================================================================
III. HIPAA COMPLIANCE PROGRAM — GAP ANALYSIS
================================================================================

The base engagement materials call for identification of deficiencies, risks, and recommended remediation in the Healthcare Data Privacy Compliance Program. The following issue set constitutes the gap analysis deliverable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Governance, Accountability, and Written Policies
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deficiency:
- Privacy Officer and Security Official designations are incomplete or not operationalized (no current charter, escalation matrix, or documented authority to compel remediation across business units and vendors).
- Enterprise privacy and security policies exist in outline form but are not version-controlled, not mapped to 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.308, 164.310, 164.312, 164.314, and 164.530, and lack evidence of periodic management review and approval.
- No integrated compliance committee cadence tying privacy, security, clinical operations, and contracting.

Risk:
- Structural HIPAA noncompliance; difficulty demonstrating "reasonable and appropriate" administrative safeguards in an OCR investigation.
- Weak tone-at-the-top defense if a reportable breach or complaint arises during or after the transaction.
- Amplifies indemnification and MAE risk given Schedule 3.7 pending regulatory inquiries.

Remediation:
1. Formally designate (or reaffirm) Privacy Officer and Security Official with written authority, budget line, and direct reporting to senior management / board risk committee.
2. Adopt a controlled policy suite covering Privacy Rule uses/disclosures, minimum necessary, Security Rule safeguard families, breach notification, sanctions, and complaint handling; assign owners and annual review dates.
3. Institute quarterly compliance reporting with metrics (access requests aging, BA inventory status, risk-analysis findings closed, training completion).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
B. Enterprise Risk Analysis and Risk Management (Security Rule)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deficiency:
- No current, enterprise-wide security risk analysis meeting the rigor expected under 45 C.F.R. § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) (asset inventory incomplete; ePHI data flows not fully mapped across cloud, EHR, analytics, and research environments).
- Risk-management plan lacks prioritized treatment of high/critical findings, residual-risk acceptance documentation, and linkage to capital / operating budgets.
- Penetration testing / vulnerability management cadence is ad hoc rather than risk-based and continuous.

Risk:
- Primary driver of OCR civil monetary penalties and resolution agreements; also the factual predicate most likely to be tested against security-related representations in the deal.
- Undocumented residual risk undermines "reasonable safeguards" defense and complicates cyber insurance placement/renewal.
- Interacts adversely with any MAE carve-out for regulatory action (see Section IV.B).

Remediation:
1. Commission (or update within 60 days) a scoped HIPAA security risk analysis covering all systems that create, receive, maintain, or transmit ePHI, including subcontractors and research platforms.
2. Produce a written risk-management plan with owners, due dates, and residual-risk sign-off for items not fully mitigated before closing or within an agreed post-closing period.
3. Align technical testing (VA/PT, configuration baselines, encryption at rest/in transit validation) to the risk register.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C. Workforce Training, Sanctions, and Minimum Necessary
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deficiency:
- Role-based HIPAA training is not consistently completed for new hires, contractors, and privileged clinical/research roles within required timeframes; refresher training is not reliably documented.
- Sanctions policy is generic and not evidenced by applied discipline logs (redacted) sufficient to show enforcement.
- Minimum-necessary standard is stated in policy but not engineered into access provisioning, query tools, or disclosure workflows.

Risk:
- Recurrent root cause in breach and complaint matters; workforce snooping and over-disclosure events.
- Weakens position in any post-closing indemnity claim predicated on pre-closing compliance representations.

Remediation:
1. Enforce role-based onboarding and annual refresher training with LMS completion attestations retained for at least six years.
2. Operationalize sanctions with consistent application and privileged documentation.
3. Implement technical and procedural minimum-necessary controls (role templates, break-glass auditing, disclosure checklists).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
D. Business Associate and Downstream Vendor Management
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deficiency:
- Business Associate Agreement ("BAA") inventory is incomplete; certain cloud, billing, analytics, telehealth, and research vendors handling PHI lack current BAAs or have non-standard terms missing required 45 C.F.R. § 164.504(e) elements (including breach reporting timelines and downstream flow-downs).
- No systematic due diligence / security questionnaire program for high-risk vendors; SOC 2 / HITRUST evidence not centrally tracked against contract obligations.
- Subcontractor flow-down and termination-for-cause rights for HIPAA material breach are uneven.

Risk:
- Direct HIPAA liability pathway for covered entity failures to obtain satisfactory assurances; contractual gap if a vendor-caused breach occurs.
- Silent shift of retained vendor-related liabilities under Schedule 5.2 if indemnification economics are weakened (see Section IV.A).

Remediation:
1. Complete BA/vendor inventory within 30 days; execute or amend BAAs to firm-standard required elements.
2. Tier vendors by PHI volume/sensitivity; require security evidence and right-to-audit for Tier 1.
3. Map vendor obligations to the risk-management plan and incident-response runbooks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
E. Access Controls, Audit Controls, and Integrity / Transmission Security
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deficiency:
- Unique user identification and automatic logoff are inconsistent on legacy clinical and shared-workstation environments.
- Audit controls do not comprehensively log access, export, and administrative actions against ePHI repositories; log review is reactive rather than risk-based.
- Encryption and integrity controls are uneven for backups, portable media, and certain interfaces; key management documentation is thin.

Risk:
- Elevated breach likelihood and delayed detection; common OCR citation cluster under §§ 164.312(a)–(e).
- Forensic gaps impair breach risk assessment under the four-factor test (§ 164.402) and can force broader notification.

Remediation:
1. Standardize identity and access management (unique IDs, MFA for remote/privileged access, joiner-mover-leaver).
2. Enable immutable / centralized logging for ePHI systems with documented review procedures and alerting.
3. Complete encryption baseline for data at rest and in transit; document compensating controls only with formal risk acceptance.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
F. Breach Detection, Incident Response, and Notification
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deficiency:
- Incident response plan is not HIPAA-specific: unclear roles for Privacy Officer involvement, four-factor risk assessment worksheets, and decision authority for breach vs. non-breach determinations.
- Notification playbooks do not reliably meet 60-day outer bound to individuals and HHS, or expedited media notice thresholds; state-law overlays are not matrixed.
- Tabletop exercises either have not been run in the current annual cycle or omit business associate coordination.

Risk:
- Late or incomplete notification is an independent violation and multiplies enforcement exposure and reputational harm.
- Directly relevant to pending regulatory inquiries on Schedule 3.7 and to any MAE formulation that carves out regulatory action.

Remediation:
1. Adopt a HIPAA-aligned IR/breach procedure with decision trees, documentation templates, and counsel escalation triggers.
2. Maintain a multi-jurisdiction notification matrix (HIPAA + state).
3. Conduct and document at least annual tabletops including a BA-caused incident scenario; remediate exercise findings.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
G. Individual Rights (Access, Amendment, Accounting) and Notice of Privacy Practices
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deficiency:
- Right-of-access fulfillment exceeds regulatory timeframes in a material subset of requests; fulfillment pathways for electronic access and third-party directives are inconsistent with current OCR enforcement emphasis.
- Notice of Privacy Practices may be outdated relative to actual uses/disclosures (research, AI/analytics, marketing/fundraising boundaries).
- Accounting of disclosures process is manual and incomplete for non-TPO disclosures.

Risk:
- Right-of-access initiative remains a high-frequency OCR enforcement area; civil monetary penalties and corrective action plans are common.
- NPP inaccuracies create separate Privacy Rule exposure and patient-trust issues.

Remediation:
1. Stand up an access-request SLA dashboard (intake → identity verification → fulfillment) with escalation before day 30.
2. Refresh NPP and acknowledgment workflows to match real data uses; train front-line staff.
3. Implement tracked accounting for non-TPO disclosures.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
H. Physical Safeguards, Device / Media Controls, and Facility Access
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deficiency:
- Device and media controls (wipe/destruction certificates, secure re-use, lost-device response) are incomplete for endpoints used in hybrid clinical and remote settings.
- Facility access controls and visitor management vary by site; contingency operations documentation is stale.

Risk:
- Device loss remains a leading breach vector; weak media sanitation undermines disposal defenses.

Remediation:
1. Enforce MDM/endpoint encryption, remote wipe, and certified media destruction.
2. Update facility access and contingency documentation; test data backup restoration on a defined cadence (§ 164.308(a)(7)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I. Research, Life-Sciences-Specific, and Hybrid-Entity Considerations
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deficiency (practice-area specific):
- Unclear segregation of covered health care components vs. research/pharma functions if hybrid-entity or affiliated covered entity structures apply; PHI vs. de-identified / limited data set pathways are not consistently gated.
- Data use agreements for limited data sets and IRB/privacy-board waiver documentation are not centrally inventoried.
- Secondary use of clinical data for analytics/AI lacks a documented legal basis matrix (TPO, authorization, waiver, de-identification under § 164.514).

Risk:
- Life-sciences data reuse is a frequent source of "impermissible use/disclosure" findings and class/consumer claims under state law.
- Heightens representation and MAE sensitivity where regulators are already inquiring (Schedule 3.7).

Remediation:
1. Map legal entity and hybrid designations; document firewall and shared-service arrangements.
2. Inventory DUAs, authorizations, and waivers; block production use of PHI for secondary purposes without a documented basis.
3. Require privacy-by-design review for AI/analytics projects touching clinical data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
J. Consolidated Risk Rating (Program)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Domain                              | Gap Severity | Deal / Enforcement Sensitivity |
|-------------------------------------|--------------|--------------------------------|
| Governance & policies               | High         | High                           |
| Risk analysis / risk management     | Critical     | Critical                       |
| Workforce training & minimum necessary | High      | Medium-High                    |
| BA / vendor management              | High         | High (Schedule 5.2 interaction)|
| Access & audit controls             | High         | High                           |
| Breach IR & notification            | Critical     | Critical (Schedule 3.7)        |
| Individual rights / NPP             | Medium-High  | Medium                         |
| Device/media & physical             | Medium-High  | Medium                         |
| Research / secondary use            | High         | High (life sciences)           |

Overall residual program risk prior to remediation: HIGH, with CRITICAL items in risk analysis and breach response that should be treated as closing or immediate post-closing conditions in any transaction context.

================================================================================
IV. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP — FULL DEVIATION RECONCILIATION
================================================================================

The counterparty's revision accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces the deviations below. Each is reconciled against the base healthcare life sciences materials and the controlling schedules/exhibits. Every deviation is addressed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEVIATION 1 — Indemnification Cap Reduced; Basket Converted Deductible → Tipping
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

What the markup does:
- Silently reduces the indemnification cap below the level reflected in the base materials / firm-standard economics.
- Converts the loss basket from a deductible (true threshold; only amounts above the basket are recoverable) to a tipping (first-dollar once threshold is exceeded) basket.

Base materials position:
- Operative agreement structure contemplates negotiated indemnification with a deductible basket and a cap calibrated to the risk allocation for compliance, privacy, and regulatory matters.

Intersecting schedule:
- Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities. The markup's indemnification changes would silently shift economics around those retained liabilities: a lower cap truncates recovery just as tipping-basket mechanics may accelerate or reshape first-dollar exposure in ways not underwritten in the base deal model. Net effect can be a transfer of residual HIPAA / privacy liability cost to the client without express pricing or disclosure.

Deficiencies / risks if accepted as drafted:
- Under-compensates for program gaps identified in Section III (especially BA/vendor and breach events).
- Creates mismatch between scheduled retained liabilities and actual recoverable indemnity.
- "Silent" cap reduction is a process defect (inadequate redline transparency) and a substance defect (unpriced risk transfer).

Recommended remediation / negotiating position:
1. Restore the base cap or, if any reduction is commercial, require express call-out, quantum justification, and special indemnity or escrow for privacy/security/regulatory matters outside the general cap.
2. Basket: if commercial pressure requires movement, document the conversion expressly; model expected loss distribution. Do not accept silent drafting. Prefer retaining deductible treatment for ordinary claims, with any tipping mechanic limited to fundamental or fraud claims only—if tipping is conceded on the general basket, pair it with a higher cap or a carve-out special indemnity for HIPAA/data-privacy breaches and Schedule 5.2 items.
3. Add an express schedule-to-indemnity cross-walk so Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities cannot be eroded by general cap/basket mechanics without written agreement.
4. Require that privacy/security breach losses (notification, credit monitoring, regulatory fines/penalties to the extent insurable/indemnifiable, and mandated corrective-action costs) be defined as recoverable losses and, where possible, subject to special indemnity treatment given program gap severity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEVIATION 2 — MAE Definition Adds Carve-Outs for Regulatory Action
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

What the markup does:
- Amends the definition of Material Adverse Effect to add carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter (i.e., privacy/security/HIPAA-oriented regulatory scrutiny and related governmental actions).

Base materials position:
- MAE is a core closing and walk-away condition without a specialized free pass for the regulatory category that is the central compliance risk of the asset.

Intersecting schedule:
- Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect these carve-outs. If MAE excludes the consequences of such regulatory action, the buyer/client may be forced to close (or lose MAE-based remedies) even if the inquiries ripen into material enforcement, CMPs, expansive corrective action plans, or operational restrictions.

Deficiencies / risks if accepted as drafted:
- Nullifies MAE protection for the precise risk disclosed on Schedule 3.7 and for the CRITICAL program gaps (risk analysis; breach response) most likely to draw OCR or state AG action.
- Converts a disclosed, live regulatory overhang into a largely non-actionable closing risk.
- Asymmetric: seller retains ability to argue that even severe HIPAA enforcement is "carved out" of MAE.

Recommended remediation / negotiating position:
1. Reject broad regulatory-action carve-outs as applied to HIPAA, state health-privacy, consumer protection, and AG investigations relating to PHI/ePHI.
2. If any regulatory carve-out is commercially unavoidable, limit it to industry-wide rules of general applicability, and expressly preserve MAE treatment for: (a) entity-specific investigations, (b) matters disclosed on Schedule 3.7 and any evolution thereof, (c) resolution agreements, CIAs, or equivalent, and (d) material expansion of the two pending inquiries.
3. Pair with enhanced interim operating covenants: cooperation, no voluntary broadening of inquiry scope, prompt notice, and consent rights before material submissions.
4. Consider a specific closing condition or special termination right tied to adverse developments in the Schedule 3.7 inquiries, independent of the general MAE definition.
5. Align bring-down of privacy/security compliance representations with Schedule 3.7 so that adverse inquiry developments remain actionable even if MAE is compromised.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEVIATION 3 — Limitation Period Shortens Survival for Core Representations
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

What the markup does:
- Introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations, including (as relevant here) compliance, privacy, security, and related regulatory representations.

Base materials position:
- Survival calibrated to allow discovery of latent compliance defects (HIPAA gaps often surface post-closing through incidents, audits, or regulator contact).

Intersecting exhibit:
- Exhibit B sets the survival matrix. The markup's limitation-period change contradicts Exhibit B. Under the schedules/exhibits rule stated in the matter file, scheduled exceptions and the exhibit matrix control over general statements—and the markup cannot be read to override Exhibit B without express amendment of that exhibit.

Deficiencies / risks if accepted as drafted:
- Time-bars indemnity claims for precisely the categories of breach most likely to be discovered after operational integration (access failures, BA gaps, risk-analysis shortfalls, secondary-use issues).
- Direct conflict with Exhibit B creates interpretive ambiguity that counterparties may exploit to argue shorter survival controls.
- In combination with a reduced cap and MAE regulatory carve-outs, shortened survival is a compounding risk transfer.

Recommended remediation / negotiating position:
1. Reject any survival reduction that contradicts Exhibit B. Require the markup to conform to Exhibit B or to amend Exhibit B only by express, bilateral revision with the same approval level as the main agreement.
2. Preserve elongated survival (or survival through applicable statute of limitations) for fundamental representations and for healthcare regulatory / HIPAA / privacy / security / compliance representations and any Schedule 3.7-related representations.
3. Clarify claim-notice mechanics (tolling upon timely notice; relation-back for related facts) so that shortened ordinary-course survival, if any, cannot trap known regulatory trajectories.
4. Do not trade survival reduction against basket concessions without express client authority; survival for core compliance representations should be treated as a non-concede / walk-away tier item relative to basket mechanics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
V. CROSS-EFFECT ANALYSIS (MARKUP × PROGRAM GAPS × SCHEDULES)
================================================================================

The three markup deviations are not independent of the HIPAA program gaps:

1. Cap ↓ + tipping basket + Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities
   → Financial recovery for pre-closing privacy/security failures becomes both smaller (cap) and differently timed (basket), while retained liabilities stay on the schedule. Net under-indemnification for Section III gaps.

2. MAE regulatory carve-outs + Schedule 3.7 pending inquiries + weak risk analysis / IR
   → Highest-probability path to "material" harm is regulatory escalation. Carving that path out of MAE while program CRITICAL gaps remain open is an unacceptable stacking of risk.

3. Shortened survival vs. Exhibit B + latent HIPAA defects
   → Program gaps (especially BA inventory, risk analysis, secondary use) are latent. Shorter survival expires before latent defects typically manifest, contradicting Exhibit B and gutting post-closing remedies.

Collectively, accepting all three deviations while program CRITICAL items remain open would leave the client with diminished closing protection, diminished post-closing recovery, and undiminished operational/regulatory exposure. That combination is outside market-reasonable risk allocation for a healthcare life sciences data-privacy-sensitive deal.

================================================================================
VI. RECOMMENDED REMEDIATION PLAN (INTEGRATED)
================================================================================

A. Immediate (pre-signing / pre-closing) — Deal Terms

1. Redline response rejecting: (i) silent cap reduction; (ii) unrestricted MAE carve-outs for entity-specific regulatory action and Schedule 3.7 matters; (iii) any survival period that contradicts Exhibit B or shortens core compliance/privacy/security representations.
2. Require express conformity of indemnification language to Schedule 5.2 (no silent shift of retained liabilities).
3. Demand clean comparison pages for all indemnification, MAE, and survival edits (cure the "silent" drafting defect).
4. Insert interim covenants and notice rights covering the two Schedule 3.7 inquiries.
5. Condition closing on delivery of: current BA inventory certification; written security risk-analysis status; and IR/breach plan update.

B. Near-Term (0–90 days) — Program CRITICAL Path

1. Enterprise HIPAA security risk analysis update and risk-management plan (owners, dates, residual-risk log).
2. HIPAA-specific incident response / breach notification procedure + tabletop.
3. Complete BAA execution/amendment for all PHI vendors; Tier-1 security evidence file.
4. Privacy Officer / Security Official charters and compliance committee stand-up.
5. Right-of-access workflow fix to stop aging breaches of regulatory deadlines.

C. Medium-Term (90–180 days) — Program HIGH Path

1. Policy suite version control mapped to regulatory citations; sanctions evidence protocol.
2. IAM/MFA/logging baseline on all ePHI systems; encryption gaps closed or formally risk-accepted.
3. Research/secondary-use legal-basis matrix and DUA/authorization inventory.
4. Device/media controls and backup-restoration testing.
5. NPP refresh and workforce role-based training completion to 100% of in-scope personnel.

D. Documentation / Evidence Hygiene

- Retain risk analyses, training logs, BAAs, IR tabletops, sanctions records, and access-request metrics for at least six years.
- Prepare an evidence binder suitable for OCR inquiry response and for any post-closing indemnity claim under the survival matrix in Exhibit B.

================================================================================
VII. ISSUE-BY-ISSUE DISPOSITION TABLE
================================================================================

| # | Issue | Source | Deficiency | Risk | Disposition / Remediation |
|---|--------|--------|------------|------|---------------------------|
| 1 | Governance / PO-SO authority | Program materials | Incomplete designation & reporting | High enforcement & culture risk | Formal charters; committee cadence |
| 2 | Policies not mapped / controlled | Program materials | Nonconforming admin safeguards | High | Adopt controlled HIPAA policy suite |
| 3 | Security risk analysis stale/incomplete | Program materials | § 164.308(a)(1) gap | Critical | New enterprise R.A. + RM plan ≤60 days |
| 4 | Training / sanctions / min necessary | Program materials | Workforce & access design gaps | High | LMS + sanctions log + role templates |
| 5 | BA inventory & BAA terms | Program materials | § 164.504(e) assurances incomplete | High; interacts w/ Sch. 5.2 | Full inventory; amend BAAs; tier diligence |
| 6 | Access, audit, encryption | Program materials | § 164.312 gaps | High | IAM/MFA/logging/encryption baseline |
| 7 | Breach IR & notification | Program materials | Process & timing defects | Critical; interacts w/ Sch. 3.7 | HIPAA IR plan; matrix; tabletop |
| 8 | Individual rights / NPP | Program materials | Access SLA & NPP drift | Medium-High | Access dashboard; NPP refresh |
| 9 | Device/media / contingency | Program materials | Loss & restoration gaps | Medium-High | MDM/wipe; restore tests |
| 10 | Research / secondary use | Program materials (life sciences) | Legal-basis & hybrid gaps | High | Entity map; DUA/auth inventory; AI review gate |
| 11 | Indemnification cap reduced (silent) | Counterparty markup | Unpriced risk transfer | High financial | Restore cap or special indemnity; end silence |
| 12 | Basket deductible → tipping | Counterparty markup | Economics shift | Medium-High; Sch. 5.2 | Express only; model; pair with cap/special indemnity |
| 13 | MAE regulatory-action carve-outs | Counterparty markup | Removes protection for core risk | Critical w/ Sch. 3.7 | Reject or narrowly limit; protect Sch. 3.7 path |
| 14 | Shortened survival / limitation | Counterparty markup | Contradicts Exhibit B; time-bars latent HIPAA claims | Critical | Conform to Exhibit B; elongated survival for compliance reps |
| 15 | Sch. 3.7 — two pending regulatory inquiries | Schedules | Live regulator overhang | Critical with Dev. 2 | Carve back into MAE; interim covenants; closing condition |
| 16 | Sch. 5.2 — retained liabilities | Schedules | Silent shift via Dev. 1 | High | Indemnity cross-walk; no silent shift |
| 17 | Exhibit B — survival matrix | Schedules/Exhibits | Conflicts with Dev. 3 | Critical interpretive | Exhibit B controls; express amend only |

All counterparty deviations (items 11–14) and all schedule/exhibit intersections (items 15–17) are addressed above. No markup deviation remains unreconciled.
